shots.src: World Bank · GDP per capita (current US$)
shots.narration: On paper, Ireland is one of the richest countries on Earth. {p} In 2024, its economy produced about a hundred and thirteen thousand dollars per person. {p} That's more than the United States. {p} It's double Germany. {p} In the whole European Union, only tiny Luxembourg ranks higher.

But walk around Dublin and ask people if they feel richer than Americans. {pp} You'll get a laugh. {p} Prices are the third highest in the EU. And the average Irish household doesn't live twice as well as a German one. {p} So which is it? {p} Is Ireland rich? <soft>Or is something strange going on with the number?</soft>

shots.src: World Bank · GDP per capita (current US$) · EU/IMF programme for Ireland (Nov 2010)
shots.narration: Ireland wasn't always the rich kid. {p} In 1990, it was poorer than the average EU country. {p} Then came the Celtic Tiger. Foreign tech and drug companies poured in, and through the late nineties, the economy often grew close to ten percent a year. {p} By 2007, Irish GDP per person was about eighty percent above the EU average. {pp} Then the housing bubble burst. The banks collapsed, and in 2010, Ireland needed an eighty-five billion euro rescue from the EU and the IMF.

shots.src: World Bank · GDP growth (annual %) · CSO (12 Jul 2016)
shots.narration: Ireland recovered. And then came the moment the number broke. {p} In 2015, according to the official statistics, Ireland's economy grew by almost twenty-five percent. {p} In one year. {pp} Rich countries don't do that. A good year is two or three percent.

shots.src: Irish Fiscal Advisory Council via Irish Examiner (8 Sep 2016) · Paul Krugman (Jul 2016)
shots.title: What happened in 2015
shots.narration: No one in Ireland got twenty-five percent richer. {p} What happened was on paper. A handful of giant multinationals, above all Apple, moved their intellectual property onto Irish books: patents, designs, the rights to their brands. {p} Ireland's capital stock jumped by about three hundred billion euros, in a single year. {p} The economist Paul Krugman gave it a name. {pp} Leprechaun economics.

items.text: capital stock: +€300 billion in one year

shots.src: Irish corporation tax 12.5% (since 2003); 15% for groups over €750m (Pillar Two, 2024)
shots.narration: Why Ireland? {p} For decades, its corporate tax rate was twelve and a half percent, one of the lowest in the rich world. {p} Since 2024, the biggest companies pay fifteen, under a global minimum tax deal. {p} Still low. {p} So companies route their profits through Ireland, often from sales made everywhere else.

shots.src: CSO; Fiscal Council (2025) · contract manufacturing in national accounts
shots.narration: And once the profits are booked in Ireland, they show up in Irish GDP. {p} A phone designed in California and assembled in China can count as an Irish export, because an Irish subsidiary owns the rights. {p} The money passes through, gets counted, {pp} and then most of it leaves again, as profits paid back to foreign owners. {p} Economists call this profit shifting, and by most estimates, Ireland is one of the biggest destinations for it in the world.

shots.src: Irish Budget 2015 (Oct 2014) · Reuters (3 Jan 2019): Google, Dutch filings for 2017
shots.title: The Double Irish
shots.narration: For years, the most famous trick had a name straight out of a spy novel: the Double Irish. {p} A company set up two Irish subsidiaries, one of them run from a tax haven like Bermuda, and passed its profits between them, often through the Netherlands. {p} Google used it to move billions through Ireland and on to Bermuda. {p} Ireland shut the Double Irish to newcomers in 2015, and closed it completely by 2020.

items.text: 2017 · Google: €19.9B to Bermuda via a Dutch shell

shots.src: European Commission decision (30 Aug 2016) · EU Court of Justice, C-465/20 P (10 Sep 2024)
shots.title: Apple vs the EU
shots.narration: And then there's Apple. {p} In 2016, the European Commission found that Apple's main Irish company had paid an effective tax rate as low as zero point zero zero five percent, in 2014. {p} It ordered Ireland to collect thirteen billion euros in back taxes. {p} Ireland fought that order in court for eight years. {pp} It didn't want the money. {p} In 2024, the EU's top court said: take it anyway.

stats.label: Apple's effective tax rate in Ireland, 2014

shots.src: Revenue / Irish Times (6 Jan 2026) · Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (2025)
shots.title: Who pays Ireland's corporate tax
shots.narration: To be clear, Ireland does collect real money from this. {p} In 2025, corporate tax brought in thirty-four point seven billion euros, almost a third of all tax revenue. {p} But it's incredibly concentrated. Just ten company groups paid fifty-six percent of it.

By 2017, even Ireland's own statisticians had had enough. {p} GDP had stopped describing the Irish economy. {p} So the Central Statistics Office invented a new number, just for Ireland. {pp} They call it modified gross national income, or GNI star. {p} It's not perfect, but Ireland's own government now uses it to measure things like the national debt.

items.text: So Ireland invented a new one:

shots.src: CSO Ireland, Annual National Accounts 2025 (2 Jul 2026)
shots.title: Ireland, 2025: GDP vs GNI*
shots.narration: GNI star strips out the profits that leave the country, and the paper value of all that foreign-owned intellectual property wearing out. {p} In 2025, Ireland's GDP was six hundred and two billion euros. {p} GNI star? Three hundred thirty-four billion. {p} About two hundred sixty-eight billion euros, roughly forty-five percent of the economy, {pp} either leaves the country or only exists on paper.

shots.src: CSO Ireland, Annual National Accounts 2025 (2 Jul 2026) · population April 2025: 5,458,600 (CSO)
shots.title: Per person, 2025
shots.narration: Per person, that's a huge difference. {p} GDP says about a hundred and ten thousand euros per Irish resident. {p} GNI star says about sixty-one thousand. {pp} Still a rich country. {p} Just not the richest. {p} In most rich countries, GDP and national income are within a few percent of each other. In Ireland, the gap is close to half.

shots.src: Eurostat prc_ppp_ind · volume indices per capita in PPS (EU27 = 100) · GDP
shots.narration: But even GNI star measures income, not living standards. {p} For that, Europe's statisticians have a better measure: actual individual consumption. {p} It counts everything households actually use: food, rent, cars, holidays, and public services like health and schools. {p} First, here's GDP per person, adjusted for prices. Ireland is more than twice the EU average. Only Luxembourg is higher.

shots.src: Eurostat prc_ppp_ind · volume indices per capita in PPS (EU27 = 100) · actual individual consumption
shots.narration: Now, here's what people actually consume. {pp} Ireland drops to ninety-nine. {p} Just below the EU average. {p} Below Germany, below France, below Belgium. {p} Back in 2006, at the height of the Celtic Tiger boom, it was a hundred and seventeen. {p} Today, the country with the second highest GDP per person in the EU ranks tenth for how its people actually live.

That doesn't mean Irish people are poor. {p} Wages are high, and the multinationals do employ hundreds of thousands of people. {p} But the headline number is mostly about where giant companies keep their accounts. {pp} <soft>Not about how much richer the Irish are than everyone else.</soft>

items.text: GDP ≈ where companies keep their books

shots.src: CSO goods exports 2025 · Euronews (4 May 2026) · CSO quarterly national accounts Q1–Q2 2026
shots.title: The catch
shots.narration: And that makes Ireland's official numbers wildly unstable. {p} In 2025, GDP grew twelve percent, while the domestic economy grew about five. {p} Pharmaceuticals drove it: exports of weight-loss drug ingredients, many rushed to the US ahead of new American tariffs. Exports to America jumped fifty-two percent. {p} Then, in early 2026, GDP fell about seven percent in three months, {p} and jumped ten percent in the next three. {pp} Meanwhile, the domestic economy just kept growing at a normal pace.

Ireland's government knows the corporate tax money could vanish if a few companies change their plans. {p} So it has started putting billions into two savings funds, instead of spending all of it. {p} Because in an economy where ten companies pay more than half the corporate tax, {pp} <soft>the leprechaun can always leave.</soft>

So, is Ireland the richest country in Europe? {p} By GDP, almost: second only to Luxembourg. {p} By what people actually consume, it's ninety-nine. Average. {pp} The truth is somewhere in between: a genuinely prosperous country, {p} with a giant corporate tax machine bolted on top.

items.text: Prosperous + a tax machine on top

yt.title: Ireland Is the Richest Country in Europe. It Isn't.
yt.description:
On paper, Ireland produces more per person than the United States. In 2015 its economy "grew" 26% in a year. What leprechaun economics is, how multinational profits inflate Irish GDP, the number Ireland invented to fix it (GNI*), and how the Irish actually live compared with the rest of Europe.
